rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Quantity of heat is the energy transferred due to temperature difference. Specific heat capacity, heat capacity, latent heat, and calorimetry principle govern heat transfer calculations. Q = mcΔT for temperature change and Q = mL for phase change.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Heat transfer: Q = mcΔT
Heat capacity: C = Q/ΔT
Specific heat capacity: c = Q/(mΔT)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Heat Capacity Definition: Heat capacity C = ΔQ/ΔT is the heat required to raise temperature by 1 K. Specific heat capacity c = C/m is per unit mass (J/kg·K). Molar heat capacity Cₘ = C/n is per mole (J/mol·K).  ·  Phase Change Latent Heat: During phase change (melting, boiling), temperature is constant while heat is absorbed/released as latent heat: Q = mL. Latent heat of fusion L_f (solid↔liquid) and vaporization L_v (liquid↔gas) are material properties.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Statement 1: Heat is energy transferred due to temperature difference; SI unit is joule.  ·  Statement 2: Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔT) is the heat per unit mass per degree temperature rise.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Heat needed to raise 2 kg water from 20°C to 80°C: Q = mcΔT = 2 × 4186 × 60 = 502,320 J ≈ 502 kJ.  ·  Heat to melt 0.5 kg ice at 0°C: Q = mL_f = 0.5 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 167,000 J = 167 kJ.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Confusing heat capacity (for whole body) with specific heat capacity (per unit mass).  ·  Thinking temperature rises during phase change: Temperature stays constant during melting/boiling.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Heat: Energy transferred between bodies due to temperature difference. SI unit: joule (J). Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.  ·  Heat Capacity: C = Q/ΔT is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K (or 1°C). Unit: J/K. Depends on mass and material of the body.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Q = mcΔT — use for temperature change (no phase change).  ·  Q = mL — use for phase change (constant temperature).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define specific heat capacity and give its SI unit.  ·  Q2. Calculate heat required to raise 3 kg of water from 25°C to 75°C.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: NEB frequently asks calorimetry numericals: mixing hot and cold bodies to find equilibrium temperature.  ·  Specific heat determination by method of mixtures is a standard experiment.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.  ·  Specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔT) is a characteristic property of material.  ·  Water has high specific heat (4186 J/kg·K) — moderates climate.  ·  During phase change, temperature remains constant despite heat absorption.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Water has one of the highest specific heat capacities among common substances (4186 J/kg·K).  ·  James Prescott Joule established the mechanical equivalent of heat: 1 cal = 4.186 J.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. State the principle of calorimetry and its assumptions.  ·  Q4. What is latent heat of fusion? How does it differ from latent heat of vaporization?  ·  Q5. A 500 g metal block at 100°C is placed in 200 g water at 20°C. Find equilibrium temperature.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Latent heat numericals: ice-steam mixtures with phase changes are common.  ·  Distinguish between specific heat (per unit mass) and heat capacity (for the whole body).

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: 200 g copper (c = 385 J/kg·K) at 100°C mixed with 300 g water at 20°C: equilibrium T found by m_cu c_cu (100-T) = m_w c_w (T-20).  ·  Heat to vaporize 0.1 kg water at 100°C: Q = mL_v = 0.1 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 226,000 J = 226 kJ.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Specific Heat Capacity: c = C/m = Q/(mΔT) is the heat required to raise unit mass of a substance by 1 K. Unit: J/(kg·K). Characteristic property of the material.  ·  Molar Heat Capacity: Cₘ = C/n = Q/(nΔT) is heat per mole. Unit: J/(mol·K). Used in thermodynamics and kinetic theory.  ·  Calorimetry Principle: In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies. Assumes no heat loss to surroundings.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Molar heat capacity: Cₘ = Q/(nΔT)  ·  Latent heat: Q = mL  ·  Specific latent heat: L = Q/m

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Calorimetry: m₁c₁(T_f - T₁) = m₂c₂(T₂ - T_f) (heat lost = heat gained)  ·  Calorimetry Principle: In an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies = heat gained by cold bodies. This assumes no heat loss to surroundings and no phase changes unless accounted for. The final equilibrium temperature is found by equating m₁c₁(T_f - T₁) = m₂c₂(T₂ - T_f).  ·  Calorimetry: heat lost = heat gained in an isolated system.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Latent heat of fusion L_f for melting; latent heat of vaporization L_v for boiling.  ·  Believing heat and temperature are the same: Heat is energy; temperature is degree of hotness.  ·  Forgetting to convert units: mass to kg, temperature to K or °C (ΔT same in both), energy to J.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Assuming calorimetry works without insulation: Heat loss to surroundings causes error.  ·  Specific heat capacity is independent of mass — it depends only on the material.  ·  Heat capacity C depends on both mass and material of the body.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: During melting or boiling, temperature stays constant while heat is being absorbed.  ·  Latent heat of vaporization is much larger than latent heat of fusion for most substances.  ·  Calorimetry assumes perfect insulation — no heat exchange with surroundings.
